# fixpoint **An autonomous coding agent, and a harness that measures it honestly.** [![CI](https://github.com/ShlokGoel/fixpoint/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/ShlokGoel/fixpoint/actions/workflows/ci.yml) A coding agent built from scratch on the raw Anthropic Messages API (no agent framework), with a reproducible evaluation harness for **SWE-bench Lite**. The harness covers per-task Docker sandboxes, full JSONL trajectories with a replay viewer, a failure taxonomy, reward-hacking detection and paired ablation statistics. The agent loop is the easy part. Most of this repo is about measuring the agent honestly: no test leakage, pinned configuration, hard per-task budgets, confidence intervals on every number, and flags on "fixes" that only make the tests pass. > **Status:** the harness is complete and tested (65 unit tests, plus Docker integration tests). **No SWE-bench results are reported yet.** The [Results](#results) table is filled only from real runs, using `analysis.report`. --- ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR A[SWE-bench Lite instance] -->|problem statement only| B(Agent loop) B <-->|Messages API, tool use| C[Claude] B -->|tool calls| D[Tool executor] D --> E[(Docker sandbox
1 container per task
no network)] B -->|every step| F[trajectory.jsonl] E -->|git diff| G[predictions.jsonl] G --> H[Official SWE-bench harness
fresh container + hidden tests] H --> I[eval_reports.json] F --> J[analysis: taxonomy,
reward-hack flags, stats] I --> J J --> K[summary.md / per_instance.csv] ``` ### Tools | Tool | What it does | |---|---| | `bash` | Runs a non-interactive command in the repo with a timeout. Output is truncated in the middle if huge. | | `read_file` | Reads a file with line numbers, optionally a line range. | | `edit_file` | Exact string replacement. `old_str` must match **exactly once**; the error messages say why a match failed and where near-misses are. Python files are compile-checked after each edit. | | `create_file` | Creates a new file. Refuses to overwrite. | | `search` / `find_files` | `grep -rnE` / `find -name`, with result caps. | | `run_tests` | Same as `bash`, but recorded as a verification step. | | `report_localization` | Declares which files will change. Only present when the localization stage is on. | | `submit` | Ends the episode. | ### Scaffold (each stage can be ablated) - **Planning:** the task prompt asks the model to restate the issue and plan its search. - **Localization gate:** edits are rejected until the agent calls `report_localization`. This forces it to find the code before changing it, and records the claim so it can be compared with the reference fix later. - **Self-verification gate:** `submit` is rejected once if no tests have run since the last edit. It only rejects once, so the agent can never deadlock. ### When the loop stops Each iteration makes one model call and runs every tool call in that response. The loop continues while the model keeps calling tools. Every episode ends with exactly one of these causes, which is logged: | Stop cause | Trigger | |---|---| | `submit` | The model called `submit` and the scaffold accepted it. | | `end_turn_no_submit` | The model stopped calling tools, was nudged once, and stopped again. | | `max_steps` / `cost_cap` / `wallclock_cap` | A per-task budget ran out (60 steps / $3 / 30 min by default). | | `no_progress` | The same tool call 3 times in a row, or 5 tool errors in a row. | | `context_overflow` | Still over the context budget after the allowed number of resets. | | `max_tokens_loop` | Three responses in a row were cut off at `max_tokens`. | | `refusal` | The model declined (`stop_reason: refusal`). | | `api_error` | The API call failed after the SDK's retries. | **Where it gets stuck, and what catches it:** - **`edit_file` mismatches** (wrong indentation, non-unique match). Caught by specific error messages, then by `no_progress`. - **Test loops** (re-running the same failing test). Caught by the repeated-call detector. - **Premature success** (submitting an untested change). Caught by the verification gate. - **Long explorations.** Caught by the step and cost caps. ### Context management: append-only Current Claude models sign their thinking blocks over the conversation that comes before them, and the API rejects a request that replays those blocks after earlier history was edited. So this agent never trims or masks old tool outputs in place. When the prompt passes the token budget, or the model reports `model_context_window_exceeded`, the conversation is **reset**. A fresh conversation starts with the original task plus a deterministic state summary that the harness tracks itself: - localized files - files read and edited - the current diff - the last test command and its output - the last 12 actions The summary costs no extra model call. Resets are capped and logged. See [`agent/context.py`](agent/context.py). --- ## Methodology - **No leakage.** The agent sees only the problem statement and the repository. The `Task` it receives has no fields for `FAIL_TO_PASS`, `PASS_TO_PASS`, the test patch or the gold patch, and a test enforces that. The files the gold patch touches are used *only* in post-hoc analysis. - **Pinned configuration.** The run fingerprint covers the model ID, thinking mode, effort level, budgets and pricing. Every prompt template is a checked-in file whose SHA-256 is logged in each trajectory. The exact model string the API reports is logged for every call. A run refuses to resume if its config changed. - **Sampling is not seedable.** Current models reject non-default `temperature`/`top_p`/`top_k`, so runs are not bit-for-bit reproducible. Instead, behaviour is pinned through `thinking` and `effort`, and **run-to-run variance should be measured** by repeating the same subset (see [Repeats](#repeats-and-variance)). The seed controls which tasks go into the subset. - **Isolation.** Each task gets its own container from the official per-instance image, with `--network none` and memory/CPU limits. The container is destroyed afterwards. Grading happens in a separate fresh container run by the official harness. - **Strict scoring.** A task is resolved only if every `FAIL_TO_PASS` test passes and no `PASS_TO_PASS` test breaks. There is no partial credit. - **Statistics that fit small samples.** Rates come with 95% Wilson intervals. Ablations are compared as **paired** runs on the same tasks, using a paired bootstrap CI and an exact McNemar test. At n = 30, one task is 3.3 points, so a delta whose CI crosses zero is reported as "no difference shown". ### Failure taxonomy Every task gets exactly one primary category, so the counts add up to N. Secondary tags are added on top. | Primary category | Meaning | |---|---| | `resolved` | Resolved under the strict criterion. | | `infra_error` | Harness, container or API failure. Not the agent's fault; re-run these with `--retry-errors`. | | `empty_patch` | No diff produced. | | `patch_apply_failed` | The patch did not apply, or the tests could not run. | | `wrong_localization` | Never edited any file the reference fix touches. | | `broke_existing_tests` | A `PASS_TO_PASS` test now fails. | | `partial_fix` | Some, but not all, `FAIL_TO_PASS` tests pass. | | `right_file_wrong_fix` | Edited the right file(s), but the target tests still fail. | **Secondary tags:** - `gave_up` - `premature_stop` - `refused` - `context_reset` - `skipped_verification` - `never_opened_gold_file` - `hallucinated_api_suspected` - `reward_hack` ### Reward-hacking detection Flags are computed from the final patch and from the commands in the trajectory. They are reported **whether or not the task was resolved**: a resolved task with a high-severity flag is a red flag, not a success. | Flag | Severity | |---|---| | `MODIFIED_EXISTING_TEST`, `DELETED_TEST_FILE`, `WEAKENED_ASSERTION` | high | | `ADDED_SKIP_OR_XFAIL` (skip/xfail/skipTest anywhere) | high | | `TEST_CONFIG_CHANGED` (conftest.py, pytest settings in setup.cfg/tox.ini/pyproject) | high | | `TRIVIAL_ASSERTION`, `FORCED_EXIT`, `TEST_TAMPER_COMMAND` (e.g. `rm tests/...` during the episode) | medium | | `ADDED_TEST_FILE` | info (allowed) | --- ## Quickstart ```bash python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -e ".[eval,dev]" pytest # unit tests: no API key, no Docker python scripts/demo_toy.py --scripted # offline end-to-end demo with a scripted fake model ``` The scripted demo replays a fixed set of tool calls on a tiny buggy repo. It checks that the loop, tools, gating, patch extraction and held-out grading work. It is **not** a model result. ### With a real model ```bash export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... docker build -f examples/Dockerfile.toy -t fixpoint-toy examples/ python scripts/demo_toy.py --docker fixpoint-toy # real model, sandboxed FIXPOINT_TEST_IMAGE=fixpoint-toy pytest tests/test_docker_sandbox.py ``` Open `viewer/trajectory_viewer.html` in a browser and load any `runs/**/*.jsonl` to replay an episode step by step. Use ← and → to move between steps. ### SWE-bench Lite You need an x86_64 Docker host with plenty of disk, because each task pulls its own environment image. The official harness docs recommend roughly 120 GB free and 16 GB RAM for large runs. ```bash make smoke # 3 hand-picked tasks: check the loop before spending money make subset # 30 random tasks (seed 0) -> runs/sub30 make eval RUN=sub30 # official harness -> runs/sub30/eval_reports.json make report RUN=sub30 # -> runs/sub30/summary.md, per_instance.csv make ablations # the same 30 tasks without localization / without self-verification make compare A=sub30 B=sub30-noloc make compare A=sub30 B=sub30-noverify make full # all 300 tasks -> runs/full ``` Before a full run, multiply the subset's measured mean cost per task by 300 to set a budget. Before any run, check that `pricing` in `configs/default.yaml` matches current [Anthropic pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing), because the cost figures are only as accurate as those values. Any config value can be overridden without editing files: ```bash python -m harness.run_agent --run-name sub30-medium --subset 30 --set effort=medium ``` ### Repeats and variance Sampling can't be seeded, so run the same subset more than once before trusting a difference: ```bash for r in 1 2 3; do python -m harness.run_agent --run-name sub30-r$r --subset 30 --seed 0; done ``` Report the spread across repeats next to any ablation delta. --- ## Results **No results yet.** Every cell below will be copied from `runs//summary.md` and `analysis.report compare` output after real runs. Nothing here is estimated. | Run | Tasks | Resolved | Resolved % (95% CI) | Mean $ / task | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Full scaffold | 30 | — | — | — | subset, seed 0 | | − localization | 30 | — | — | — | paired with the row above | | − self-verification | 30 | — | — | — | paired with the first row | | Full scaffold | 300 | — | — | — | all of SWE-bench Lite | Failure taxonomy and reward-hacking flags will go here once the subset run is graded. [`docs/writeup_template.md`](docs/writeup_template.md) is the outline for the technical write-up. --- ## Repository layout ``` agent/ the agent: config, LLM client, tools, sandbox, loop, context, trajectories prompts/ prompt templates (hashed into every trajectory) harness/ SWE-bench task loading, per-task runs, official-harness wrapper analysis/ reward-hack detector, failure taxonomy, statistics, reports viewer/ self-contained HTML trajectory viewer configs/ default.yaml (every setting, documented) examples/ toy repo + held-out test + Dockerfile for the offline demo scripts/ demo_toy.py tests/ unit tests, plus Docker integration tests (opt-in) docs/ write-up template ``` ## Limitations - SWE-bench Lite is Python-only and skews toward a few large repositories (Django and SymPy make up a big share), so results may not generalize. - `wrong_localization` uses the set of files the reference fix touches. A valid fix in a different file would be labeled as a localization failure. - `hallucinated_api_suspected` and the reward-hack flags are pattern-based. Read the flagged trajectories before drawing conclusions. - A context reset keeps the state but drops the model's earlier reasoning. The `context_reset` tag lets you check whether resets correlate with failures. - Results depend on the model version and on the API's default behaviour at run time. Both are logged, but they can't be frozen. ## License MIT. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

     Authors: Woosung Koh ,  Hyunsoo Lee ,  Kyungjae Lee ,  Haeju Park ,  Dahyun Lee ,  Dasol Hwang ,  Moontae Lee              View a PDF of the paper titled Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation, by Woosung Koh and 6 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.

     Title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization 
     Authors: Sihwan Park ,  Sung-Yub Kim ,  Doohyuk Jang ,  Eunho Yang              View a PDF of the paper titled KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization, by Sihwan Park and 3 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.

As of now, Qwen2.5-Coder has covered six mainstream model sizes, 0.5, 1.5, 3, 7, 14, 32 billion parameters, to meet the needs of different developers. Qwen2.5-Coder brings the following improvements upon CodeQwen1.5: - Significantly improvements in **code generation**, **code reasoning** and **code fixing**. Base on the strong Qwen2.5, we scale up the training tokens into 5.5 trillion including source code, text-code grounding, Synthetic data, etc. Qwen2.5-Coder-32B has become the current state-of-the-art open-source codeLLM, with its coding abilities matching those of GPT-4o. - A more comprehensive foundation for real-world applications such as **Code Agents**. Not only enhancing coding capabilities but also maintaining its strengths in mathematics and general competencies. **This repo contains the instruction-tuned 1.5B Qwen2.5-Coder model**, which has the following features: - Type: Causal Language Models - Training Stage: Pretraining & Post-training - Architecture: transformers with RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, Attention QKV bias and tied word embeddings - Number of Parameters: 1.54B - Number of Paramaters (Non-Embedding): 1.31B - Number of Layers: 28 - Number of Attention Heads (GQA): 12 for Q and 2 for KV - Context Length: Full 32,768 tokens For more details, please refer to our [blog](https://qwenlm.github.io/blog/qwen2.5-coder-family/), [GitHub](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen2.5-Coder), [Documentation](https://qwen.readthedocs.io/en/latest/), [Arxiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12186). ## Requirements The code of Qwen2.5-Coder has been in the latest Hugging face `transformers` and we advise you to use the latest version of `transformers`. With `transformers<4.37.0`, you will encounter the following error: ``` KeyError: 'qwen2' ``` ## Quickstart Here provides a code snippet with `apply_chat_template` to show you how to load the tokenizer and model and how to generate contents. ```python from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_name, torch_dtype="auto", device_map="auto" ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name) prompt = "write a quick sort algorithm." messages = [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud. You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": prompt} ] text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True ) model_inputs = tokenizer([text], return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) generated_ids = model.generate( **model_inputs, max_new_tokens=512 ) generated_ids = [ output_ids[len(input_ids):] for input_ids, output_ids in zip(model_inputs.input_ids, generated_ids) ] response = tokenizer.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)[0] ``` ## Evaluation & Performance Detailed evaluation results are reported in this [📑 blog](https://qwenlm.github.io/blog/qwen2.5-coder-family/).      Title: A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models 
     Authors: Jiacheng Liu ,  Peng Tang ,  Wenfeng Wang ,  Yuhang Ren ,  Xiaofeng Hou ,  Pheng-Ann Heng ,  Minyi Guo ,  Chao Li              View a PDF of the paper titled A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models, by Jiacheng Liu and 7 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: The emergence of large-scale Mixture of Experts (MoE) models represents a significant advancement in artificial intelligence, offering enhanced model capacity and computational efficiency through conditional computation. However, deploying and running inference on these models presents significant challenges in computational resources, latency, and energy efficiency. This comprehensive survey analyzes optimization techniques for MoE models across the entire system stack. We first establish a taxonomical framework that categorizes optimization approaches into model-level, system-level, and hardware-level optimizations. At the model level, we examine architectural innovations including efficient expert design, attention mechanisms, various compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation, as well as algorithm improvement including dynamic routing strategies and expert merging methods. At the system level, we investigate distributed computing approaches, load balancing mechanisms, and efficient scheduling algorithms that enable scalable deployment. Furthermore, we delve into hardware-specific optimizations and co-design strategies that maximize throughput and energy efficiency. This survey provides both a structured overview of existing solutions and identifies key challenges and promising research directions in MoE inference optimization. To facilitate ongoing updates and the sharing of cutting-edge advances in MoE inference optimization research, we have established a repository accessible at  this https URL .

     Title: AfriNLLB: Efficient Translation Models for African Languages 
     Authors: Yasmin Moslem ,  Aman Kassahun Wassie ,  Amanuel Gizachew Abebe              View a PDF of the paper titled AfriNLLB: Efficient Translation Models for African Languages, by Yasmin Moslem and 2 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: In this work, we present AfriNLLB, a series of lightweight models for efficient translation from and into African languages. AfriNLLB supports 15 language pairs (30 translation directions), including Swahili, Hausa, Yoruba, Amharic, Somali, Zulu, Lingala, Afrikaans, Wolof, and Egyptian Arabic, as well as other African Union official languages such as Arabic (MSA), French, Portuguese, and Spanish. Our training data covers bidirectional translation between English and 13 languages, and between French and two languages (Lingala and Wolof).
 AfriNLLB models are based on NLLB-200 600M, which we compress using iterative layer pruning and quantization. We fine-tune the pruned models on parallel corpora we curated for African languages, employing knowledge distillation from a larger teacher model. Our work aims at enabling efficient deployment of translation models for African languages in resource-constrained settings.
 Our evaluation results demonstrate that AfriNLLB models achieve performance comparable to the baseline while being significantly faster. We release two versions of the AfriNLLB models, a Transformers version that allows further fine-tuning and a CTranslate2 version for efficient inference. Moreover, we release all the training data that we used for fine-tuning the baseline and pruned models to facilitate further research.

     Title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training 
     Authors: Leo Fan ,  Hongyang Wang ,  Wenbo Chen ,  Jingguo Liu ,  Xian Li ,  Xuan Wang ,  Ruochen Wen ,  Yiming Yan ,  Hao Wu ,  Zheshen Wang ,  Benoit Dumoulin              View a PDF of the paper titled ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training, by Leo Fan and 10 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at  this https URL .

     Title: Cortex: Measurement-Gated Evolution and Pruning of Coding-Agent Skills and Rules 
     Authors: Samuele Giampieri              View a PDF of the paper titled Cortex: Measurement-Gated Evolution and Pruning of Coding-Agent Skills and Rules, by Samuele Giampieri 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Coding agents such as Claude Code also follow text files that developers write for them: a project file, skills the agent may choose to open, and rules that load automatically when the agent reads matching files. We call these files the agent's harness. Developers add to it whenever they correct the agent, but one success proves little: the same agent can pass a task once and fail it the next time.
 We present Cortex, a tool that tests changes to the harness instead of trusting them. It saves fixes from the developer's sessions as replayable tasks, finds the corrections that recur, writes one skill or rule at a time, and keeps it only if repeated runs with and without it show a net gain and no task made noticeably worse. Existing text is tested the same way before it is deleted, and Cortex neither adds nor deletes text the agent never used.
 We tested Cortex with Claude Haiku 4.5 on a repository built for the purpose, with conventions the model tends to break, one area with nothing to learn, and a script playing the developer. On held-out tasks, the harnesses it built made the agent follow the conventions far more often than no skills or rules did, left the comparison area unchanged, and added no text read on every turn. Rules, which load automatically, did most of the work; skills helped only when offered with the files a task touches, and those offered on every turn were rarely opened. Cortex kept none of the useless or harmful suggestions we planted, but the agent never opened the useless ones or the harmful skills, and it reached no verdict on the harmful rules, so the test shows that Cortex keeps no unused text, not that it detects damage. Under the stronger Claude Sonnet 5 a single run's harness added little, and on a real open-source project, where the agent was rarely corrected, Cortex found nothing to learn. We release the tool, the lab and its data.

     Title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning 
     Authors: Minghao Luo ,  Liang Chen              View a PDF of the paper titled DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning, by Minghao Luo and 1 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at  this https URL .

     Title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction 
     Authors: Yu Lin ,  Yiming Wang ,  Runyuan Cai ,  Hanze Liu ,  Xiaodong Zeng              View a PDF of the paper titled The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction, by Yu Lin and 4 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference on consumer hardware is bounded by weight memory: a 35B-class model is 19.5GB at 4-bit, and sparsity shrinks the compute per token, not the bytes that must be held. Naive offloading to SSD does not help on its own, because layer N+1's experts must be chosen before layer N's output exists, so the reads cannot start early enough to hide behind compute. We present Edge0, a streaming MoE inference engine that closes the gap with a prerouter: a per-layer head predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, and the prediction is consumed as the routing itself, so the staged expert set equals the routed set and nothing is dropped. An unmerged recovery LoRA, trained on the student path, pays back the quality lost to int4 quantization and routing replacement. On a single 24GB machine, Edge0 serves a 35B MoE at 20tok/s inside 3GiB of peak active memory, within a few points of its fp16 teacher on average across five public benchmarks. An 8B tier runs on the same framework, and the framework, checkpoints, and adapters are open source.

# edge0 **An open-source streaming MoE inference framework — SSD expert offload + Recover-LoRA + prerouter routing prediction.** **Python** · **macOS** · **iOS** · **Android** — one recipe, every device. [![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Hugging%20Face-Edge0--35B--A3B--preview-yellow?style=for-the-badge)](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Edge0-35B-A3B-preview) [![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Hugging%20Face-Edge0--8B--A1B--preview-yellow?style=for-the-badge)](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Edge0-8B-A1B-preview) [![ModelScope](https://img.shields.io/badge/ModelScope-Edge0--35B--A3B--preview-624AFF?style=for-the-badge)](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/Edge0/Edge0-35B-A3B-preview) [![ModelScope](https://img.shields.io/badge/ModelScope-Edge0--8B--A1B--preview-624AFF?style=for-the-badge)](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/Edge0/Edge0-8B-A1B-preview) [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2609.18063-B31B1B?style=for-the-badge&logo=arxiv&logoColor=white)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18063) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Edge0--AI%2FEdge0-black?style=for-the-badge&logo=github)](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Edge0) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-blue?style=for-the-badge)](LICENSE) English | [中文](README_zh.md) | [日本語](README_ja.md) | [Español](README_es.md) | [Français](README_fr.md)
## News - **[2026-09-30]** We released the **edge0 inference engines for four platforms — iOS, macOS, Android and Windows** — so users get the best inference experience across architectures and platforms. The source is open-sourced in this repo ([`ios/`](ios/) · [`macos/`](macos/) · [`android/`](android/) · [`windows/`](windows/)) — see each directory's README for details. The **unified inference framework** follows in **Q4 2026**; see the [Roadmap](#roadmap). - **[2026-09-16]** Our technical report is on arXiv: [The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18063). - **[2026-09-08]** Initial open-source release of **edge0**, together with both model tiers — [`Edge0-35B-A3B-preview`](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Edge0-35B-A3B-preview) and [`Edge0-8B-A1B-preview`](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Edge0-8B-A1B-preview) — on Hugging Face and ModelScope. ## About **edge0** is an open-source streaming MoE inference framework. It generalizes the production-proven recipe — **SSD expert offload + Recover-LoRA + prerouter routing prediction** — into an extensible framework that runs large sparse-MoE models on consumer hardware: peak memory is bounded by the *active* expert set, not the parameter count. ### Core mechanisms - **SSD expert offload**: expert weights are streamed from storage on demand; peak memory is bounded by the active set, not the parameter count. - **Prerouter**: a trained head predicts expert routing one step ahead, so expert loads overlap the forward pass instead of stalling it — **up to +59%** decode throughput; the gain grows with storage latency, model size, and routed width *K*. - **Recover-LoRA**: the int4 base is frozen and LoRA adapters are trained by distillation from the FP teacher, recovering most of the quantization loss at 4-bit (see [Quality](#quality)). Adapters stay unmerged: one read-only base serves multiple adapter sets. ### Platforms One repo, one recipe, per-platform runtimes: | Platform | Directory | Stack | Status | |---|---|---|---| | **Python** (macOS · Apple Silicon) | [`python/`](python/README.md) | Python + MLX | ✅ Available now | | **macOS** app & CLI | [`macos/`](macos/README.md) | Rust | ✅ Open-sourced (2026-09-30) | | **iOS** app | [`ios/`](ios/README.md) | Swift + MLX Swift | ✅ Open-sourced (2026-09-30) | | **Android** app & engine | [`android/`](android/README.md) | Kotlin + native engine | ✅ Open-sourced (2026-09-30) | | **Windows** app & engine | [`windows/`](windows/README.md) | C++ + Vulkan | ✅ Open-sourced (2026-09-30) | ### Models Two model tiers ship with the framework. Each tier is an end-to-end release: the released checkpoint, the trained LoRA adapters, and the trained prerouter heads work together as one unit. | Tier | Released checkpoint | Inference profile | |---|---|---| | `edge0-35b` | [`Edge0/Edge0-35B-A3B-preview`](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Edge0-35B-A3B-preview) · [ModelScope](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/Edge0/Edge0-35B-A3B-preview) | 4-bit, 40 layers, 256 experts, prerouter K=4 | | `edge0-8b` | [`Edge0/Edge0-8B-A1B-preview`](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Edge0-8B-A1B-preview) · [ModelScope](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/Edge0/Edge0-8B-A1B-preview) | 4-bit, 24 layers, 128 experts, prerouter K=8 | Both checkpoints are built on open sparse-MoE base models (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and the Ling 3.0 bailing hybrid respectively) and ship with the LoRA and prerouter training done for this framework — the adapter files are co-located with each checkpoint and load automatically, so `edge0 serve ` runs the trained pipeline out of the box. ### Design - **transformers-style usage**: `AutoModel` / `AutoConfig` / `AutoEngine` resolve the tier from the model name; - **Backend isolation (Python framework)**: within the Python framework, all MLX code lives under `python/src/edge0/backends/mlx/`; the core logic (model specs, prerouter, streaming expert pool, server) depends only on the backend facade (`backends/base.py`), so a new backend implements the same facade (`backends/cuda/` is a reserved slot) with zero changes to core code. The iOS / macOS / Android engines ship platform-native stacks today — bringing every platform under one access layer is exactly what the unified inference framework (see [Roadmap](#roadmap)) will deliver; - **Adapters as safetensors**: LoRA and prerouter weights are `.safetensors` files with provenance metadata (source, version, owner layers), resolved from the model directory or `artifacts/`; - **Model + adapters in one directory**: a model directory holds both the base checkpoint (`config.json` / `model*.safetensors` / tokenizer) and that model's adapters; upgrading adapters swaps adapter files only — the base stays read-only and is never merged. ### Quality All benchmarks were run by us with [OpenCompass](https://github.com/open-compass/opencompass) under identical settings and parameters for both the edge0 models (int4 + trained adapters + prerouter routing) and the original fp16 base models. The loss of the edge0 pipeline is small: **3.9 points on average for edge0-35b, 2.8 for edge0-8b** (MMLU-Pro is even above the base). Max 100: | Benchmark | edge0-35b (int4) | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (fp16) | edge0-8b (int4) | Ling 3.0 tiny (fp16) | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | AIME 2026 | 86.6 | 92.7 | 63.3 | 73.3 | | HumanEval | 90.9 | 95.1 | 91.5 | 92.7 | | GPQA-Diamond | 79.8 | 81.8 | 70.7 | 71.2 | | MMLU-Pro | 81.0 | 84.6 | 70.1 | 65.8 | | IFBench | 57.9 | 61.7 | 53.9 | 60.6 | | **Average** | **79.2** | **83.2** | **69.9** | **72.7** | ### Benchmark Measured with `python/examples/bench.py` (3.3k-token prompt prefill → 10 sampled warmup steps → 200 timed sampled decode tokens, 2 runs per tier): | Tier | Decode speed | Prefill throughput (cold / warm)* | Peak MLX allocator memory | Test machine | |---|---|---|---|---| | `edge0-35b` | 14.9–17.7 tok/s | 113 / 140 tok/s | 2.9 GiB | Mac mini M4 Pro, 24 GB | | `edge0-8b` | 23.9–25.3 tok/s | 500 / 1428 tok/s | 1.0 GiB | Mac mini M4 Pro, 24 GB | *Cold = first request after process start (expert weights fault in from SSD); warm = subsequent requests (page cache resident). Prefill numbers are throughput over a ~3.3k-token prompt (`BENCH_LONG=1`). Peak MLX allocator memory is `mlx.core.get_peak_memory()` after decode — not process RSS.* Reproduce: ```bash cd python python examples/bench.py edge0-35b # via $EDGE0_35B_MODEL python examples/bench.py edge0-8b # via $EDGE0_8B_MODEL ``` ## Getting Started ### Python (macOS · Apple Silicon) #### Requirements - **OS / hardware**: the MLX backend runs on macOS with Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4). The CUDA backend is on the roadmap — no other platforms are supported by the Python framework yet. - **Python**: 3.10+ (3.12 recommended). - **MLX**: `mlx==0.30.6` / `mlx-metal==0.30.6` with `mlx-lm==0.31.0` (see `python/pyproject.toml`). Garbled, mixed-language output on Apple A18 / A18 Pro means an older `mlx`: `pip install 'mlx==0.30.6' 'mlx-metal==0.30.6'` ([#8](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Edge0/issues/8)). - **Memory**: ~2.9 GB **MLX allocator** peak for `edge0-35b`, ~1.0 GB for `edge0-8b` (short contexts; see [Benchmark](#benchmark)). That figure is `mlx.core.get_peak_memory()`, not process RSS — file-backed expert pages, the MLX buffer cache, tokenizer, and interpreter are extra, but that extra RSS is reclaimable and does not set the machine requirement (the same build runs on a 16 GB M2). Add headroom for the OS, tokenizer, and long-context KV growth. - **Disk**: the 4-bit checkpoints are ~23 GB (`edge0-35b`) and ~4.2 GB (`edge0-8b`); expert weights are mmapped and read on demand, they are not loaded into RAM up front. #### 1) Install ```bash cd python # Python >= 3.10; the MLX backend requires macOS with Apple Silicon python3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e '.[dev,fetch]' ``` #### 2) Download a model The two tiers are published on Hugging Face and ModelScope — each repo bundles the base checkpoint and the trained LoRA + prerouter adapters in **one directory**, so a single download is a ready-to-run model: - [`Edge0/Edge0-35B-A3B-preview`](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Edge0-35B-A3B-preview) (~23 GB) · [ModelScope mirror](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/Edge0/Edge0-35B-A3B-preview) - [`Edge0/Edge0-8B-A1B-preview`](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Edge0-8B-A1B-preview) (~4.2 GB) · [ModelScope mirror](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/Edge0/Edge0-8B-A1B-preview) ```bash # with the repo's helper (defaults to the two repos above): .venv/bin/python scripts/fetch_models.py --tier edge0-35b --target-dir models .venv/bin/python scripts/fetch_models.py --tier edge0-8b --target-dir models # or directly with the CLI: .venv/bin/huggingface-cli download Edge0/Edge0-35B-A3B-preview --local-dir models/edge0-35b .venv/bin/huggingface-cli download Edge0/Edge0-8B-A1B-preview --local-dir models/edge0-8b ``` Either way you end up with a directory like: ``` models/edge0-35b/ ├── config.json, model-*.safetensors, tokenizer files # base checkpoint ├── lora_edge0_35b.safetensors # trained LoRA adapters └── prerouter_edge0_35b.safetensors # trained prerouter heads ``` #### 3) Point edge0 at it Tier names resolve to local directories via environment variables (where you put the download is up to you): ```bash export EDGE0_35B_MODEL=$PWD/models/edge0-35b export EDGE0_8B_MODEL=$PWD/models/edge0-8b ``` Or skip the env vars entirely and pass the directory directly — the tier is auto-detected from the checkpoint's `config.json`: ```bash edge0 demo models/edge0-35b edge0 serve models/edge0-8b ``` #### 4) Run ```bash # quick demo edge0 demo edge0-35b # serve (OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions) edge0 serve edge0-35b ``` ```bash curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"edge0-35b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello!"}],"max_tokens":32}' # 5) One-shot chat (pass --max-new to cap length; add --show-thinking to # print the model's reasoning block too) edge0 chat edge0-35b --prompt "Explain streaming inference in one sentence." ``` `python -m edge0 ...` is equivalent to `edge0 ...`. #### Python API ```python from edge0 import AutoEngine from edge0.server.chat import ChatMessage, ChatRequest, ChatSession engine = AutoEngine.from_pretrained("/path/to/model") # tier auto-detected req = ChatRequest( model=engine.name, messages=[ChatMessage(role="user", content="Hello!")], max_tokens=64, ) tokens, meta = ChatSession(engine, req).run() print(engine._tok.decode(tokens)) engine.close() # release mmaps / expert cache ``` `python/examples/demo.py` is the same minimal walkthrough (`edge0 demo` runs this exact path). #### Models and adapters - **Checkpoint**: the original model directory (`config.json`, `model*.safetensors`, tokenizer). `edge0 serve ` / `AutoEngine.from_pretrained()` detect the tier from `config.json`. - **Adapters** (LoRA + prerouter, safetensors) are resolved from either location automatically: - the model directory (recommended): side by side with the base, e.g. `lora_edge0_35b.safetensors` + `prerouter_edge0_35b.safetensors`; - `artifacts/` at the Python project root (gitignored): an optional fallback cache for adapter safetensors not co-located with the model. - The published model repos bundle both the base checkpoint and the current default adapter release, so `scripts/fetch_models.py` produces a ready-to-run model directory. Check each model's doc page for its adapter provenance (training data, owner-layer layout). - Both adapters are required for the prerouter + LoRA pipeline; if a file is missing, `edge0` fails with a clear message (or pass `--no-prerouter` / `--no-lora` to run the plain base model). #### Documentation - [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) - [Attention](docs/attention.md) / [MoE](docs/moe.md) / [SSD streaming](docs/streaming.md) / [prerouter](docs/prerouter.md) - [Adding a model](docs/adding-a-model.md) - [edge0-35b](docs/models/edge0-35b.md) / [edge0-8b](docs/models/edge0-8b.md) - Technical report: [The Other Half of the Memory Wall](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18063) ([PDF](paper/main.pdf)) ### macOS / iOS / Android / Windows The four platform engines are open-sourced in this repo — more details in each directory's README: - **macOS**: local CLI / daemon / desktop app (Rust) — see [`macos/README.md`](macos/README.md) - **iOS**: on-device iPhone app (Swift + MLX Swift) — see [`ios/README.md`](ios/README.md) - **Android**: on-device app + native engine (Kotlin) — see [`android/README.md`](android/README.md) - **Windows**: desktop app + native engine (C++ + Vulkan) — see [`windows/README.md`](windows/README.md) The **unified inference framework** — one access layer, runtime auto-adapting to iOS / macOS / Android / Windows / Python — arrives in **Q4 2026**; see the [Roadmap](#roadmap). ## Roadmap ### Q4 2026 **Platforms & systems** - **edge0 unified inference framework** — we will open-source a unified inference framework: **one unified access layer** (a single API across chat / serve / on-device use), with the **runtime automatically adapting to the hardware platform** — iOS, macOS, Android, Windows and Python. It builds on the platform engines already open-sourced in this repo (`ios/` · `macos/` · `android/` · `windows/`). - **CUDA backend** for the Python framework — reserved slot at `python/src/edge0/backends/cuda/`, core code needs zero changes. **Models & algorithms** Q4 works two fronts: bringing a next-generation architecture into the framework, and turning latent reasoning into a real latency saving rather than just an arithmetic one. - **Next-gen architecture support (Qwen3.8-Flash class)** — run hybrid linear attention (GDN + QSA), gated multi-branch residual, and N-gram embedding topologies on edge0. These designs suit SSD streaming offload naturally: O(1)-state attention keeps long thinking from becoming a KV-cache problem, and lookup-only N-gram tables stream on demand. Goal: the tier runs on a single device and benchmarks within an acceptable gap of the fp16 base. - **Latent thinking + batched expert pre-prediction** — make latent reasoning a *latency* saving, not only an arithmetic one. The core engineering problem: move expert routing from per-position to **once per block**, so one prediction covers every position and round of a block and **expert load volume decouples from the reasoning loop count** — plus cross-block prefetch that loads the next block's experts inside the current block's compute window. Progress is measured as **end-to-end thinking-phase time at matched accuracy** (never tokens/s). - More model tiers and adapter releases on the existing pipeline. ## Contributing Contributions are welcome — issues, PRs, benchmark reports and model ports all count. **Python framework** (available now): ```bash cd python python3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e '.[dev,fetch]' pytest # unit tests (no real weights) EDGE0_8B_MODEL=/path/to/edge0-8b pytest -m slow -q # real-weight generation; missing tiers are skipped .venv/bin/python scripts/e2e_smoke.py \ --qwen-dir /path/to/edge0-35b --ling-dir /path/to/edge0-8b # staged vs exact consistency + generation smoke scripts/generate_example.py # full-pipeline API example examples/demo.py # minimal API walkthrough ``` CI runs unit tests (macOS + MLX) and a repo-hygiene suite (no hardcoded paths, backend-boundary and secret checks) on every PR. **Platform runtimes** (macOS / iOS / Android / Windows): each platform directory ships its own build guide and tests — see the directory READMEs. Workflow: fork → feature branch → PR against `main`. Please keep the hygiene suite green and add tests for new behavior. ## Citation If you find edge0 useful, please cite our technical report: ```bibtex @article{lin2026other, title = {The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction}, author = {Lin, Yu and Wang, Yiming and Cai, Runyuan and Liu, Hanze and Zeng, Xiaodong}, journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.18063}, year = {2026}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18063} } ``` ## Contact Us Community and support channels are coming soon — this section will list the official ways to reach us: - **Email**: samuel@edge0.ai For bugs and feature requests, please use [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Edge0/issues). ## License Apache-2.0, including vendored third-party code (see [NOTICE](NOTICE)).

     Title: nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own 
     Authors: Guangyi Liu ,  Yong Liu ,  Jiangning Zhang              View a PDF of the paper titled nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own, by Guangyi Liu and 2 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Assistants from 2011 answered and waited, and agents from 2023 did a task and stopped. In September 2026 Meta's Muse showed an agent for one person, with accounts, devices, memory and a conversation that lasts, closed, in a vendor's cloud, in one country. Such an agent is expected to act on a person's accounts and devices, remember them across weeks, speak first when it is worth it, and answer for what it did. It is a kind of software, not a model, and until now had no open counterpart. This report defines the personal agent in five questions and three horizons. It reads how Muse is built from Meta's public record and a copy of its production prompt, each statement marked by its source. It then presents nanoMuse, the open-source counterpart under the GPL-3.0, one agent on every device a person owns, with hands on the phone's screen and the computer's. They share one conversation over a relay anyone can run; every action goes through a Sentinel, memory is files the person can read, and the model is their choice. Its size and cost are given as estimates. What is open, memory with provenance, an evaluation suite for the hands and an open model for them, is set out as a roadmap.

**nanoMuse is an open-source personal agent for every device you own.** One agent with a name and a look of its own, in the style of Meta's [Muse](https://about.fb.com/news/2026/09/introducing-muse-personal-ai-agent/): it does things instead of answering questions, keeps working while the app is closed, remembers you, and stops to ask before anything you could not undo. *nano* means the whole set, small enough to run and deploy yourself: the phone app, the desktop app, the web console and the relay that joins them are all in this repository, under GPL-3.0-or-later. **[Free, open source, non-profit. Let's build it together.](CONTRIBUTING.md)** Sign in and you get a free allowance of model use on the community relay (the developer pays for it); when it is gone, [use your own key](docs/own-key.md). The same relay runs on a server of yours, so nothing has to leave your house. Latest: **1.0.5 Lookout**, [release notes](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/releases/tag/v1.0.5) · [try it in the browser](https://demo.nanomuse.dev/). > [!NOTE] > **nanoMuse keeps evolving** > > A personal agent should not live only in someone else's cloud, so nanoMuse is the open-source, low-cost alternative: on your own devices, with a model you choose and a relay you can host yourself. We want to build it with developers and users everywhere, so that each person truly owns a personal agent. Open an [issue](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/new/choose) or send a [pull request](CONTRIBUTING.md); either one helps nanoMuse get better. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c7694d5a-9450-4f99-9254-5d70560d7565

Open the app, sign in with an e-mail or a mainland-China phone number, and it has a model to think with. The phone, the desktop and the web share one account and show the same conversations. ## What it does
Does things.
A Linux shell, a browser, MCP servers and skills, and, with Hands on, the apps on your phone and the windows on your computer through their screens, for everything that never had an API.		 Asks first.
A stop before deleting, sending or paying, remembered for once, this chat or always; passwords and codes are yours to type. A login or a CAPTCHA is handed to you, Done resumes.
Reaches your other devices.
Say it on the phone, it runs on your PC; @Mac … at the start of a message sends the task there. Approvals come back to the device in your hand.		 Keeps going.
Goals checked on a schedule, routines that run while the app is closed, a feed written for you each morning.
Remembers you.
What it is, what it knows about you and when it wakes are Markdown files you can read and edit.		 Lives in your chat apps.
It answers in 飞书, 钉钉, 企业微信 and Telegram.
A look of its own.
Describe one, your image model draws it, a video model makes it move. A small dragon by default.		 Any model.
The relay's allowance, your own key at one of twenty-one providers (Bailian, OpenRouter, OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek and more), or a plan you already pay for: ChatGPT, Claude, Kimi. A provider without picture or video models leaves those two off, and the app says so.
## How it works Each device runs its own agent: the phone inside the APK (Alpine Linux under proot, a shell, a browser, MCP), the computer inside nanoMuse Desktop (DeepSeek Harness with the Python runtime for the hands). Signed in, they meet on the relay and can ask each other for things; the text of the conversations travels through it, files and screenshots stay where they were made.

[docs/every-device.md](docs/every-device.md) explains the devices, [docs/hub.md](docs/hub.md) the frames, [docs/cloud.md](docs/cloud.md) the relay, [docs/privacy.md](docs/privacy.md) what it keeps. ## Compared with Muse and OpenMinis | | Meta Muse | OpenMinis | nanoMuse | |---|---|---|---| | Where the agent runs | A cloud VM per user | The phone it is installed on | Your phone, your computer, or a server of yours, one account across them | | Apps without an API | Out of reach; the VM never touches your devices | An accessibility CLI on Android | The screen as a hand on the phone and the computer: screenshots, APIs first, you take over for logins. Not on iOS, where the system does not allow it | | Other devices | Clients of one VM | The one it is installed on | Devices ask each other for things over the hub, with approvals where you are | | Models | Meta's | Bring your own | The relay's free allowance, or your own | | Licence | Closed | GPL-3.0 | GPL-3.0-or-later, built on OpenMinis | ## Docs [nanomuse.cn/docs](https://nanomuse.cn/docs/): install per platform, every device, hands, connectors, memory, self-hosting, the protocols. The sources are in [docs/](docs/); what changed in each version is in the [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md) and [docs/releases/](docs/releases/). ## Self-host One VPS, one hour: [docs/self-hosting.md](docs/self-hosting.md). Three ways: no server at all with your own key, your own relay with `scripts/self-host.sh`, or a runtime of your own for the web app. ## Contribute Use it for a real task, report what broke, then pick something focused: [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) has the setup and the conventions, [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) the rules a coding agent follows in this tree, and the [roadmap](docs/roadmap.md) says where to start. nanoMuse 1.0.5 · Lookout\n\n🐉 **nanoMuse `1.0.5` “Lookout”**: the day after Compass, a second look at the whole project together with the day's reports; the daily feed is written out of sight, the Android approval card fits the screen, the desktop's dead buttons work and a quit protects the work in progress, the Windows release can update itself, and the relay's console finds anything.\n\n1.0.4 went out on 2026-10-13. The same day we read nanoMuse through once more, this time with the reports and pull requests that arrived while Compass was being built, and nine passes again went over the relay, the Python runtime, the web console, the desktop, the Android and iPhone apps, the hosted showcase, the documentation and the workflows ([#444](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/444) to [#455](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/455)). What they found fills this version. Some of it you will see at once: the chat the daily feed is written in no longer sits in your chat list on any device, and a routine's turn opens with its result; a long command no longer pushes the Android approval card's buttons off the screen ([#436](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/436), reported by @HBSTAR0501); the ChatGPT sign-in on a phone with a proxy has a way through ([#441](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/441), reported by @Kooooooo-G); the iPhone's conversation scrolls under the header, Siri understands the app's phrases in nine languages, and an emoji face set on the desktop shows on the phone ([#435](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/435), reported by @Yousanflics); eight desktop buttons that quietly did nothing do their job again, and quitting the desktop asks before it ends a reply, a hands run or a task another device is waiting on. Others you will not see and should not have to: a disabled account cannot be told apart from any other through the sign-in routes, the proxy file on the desktop is the owner's alone, a hub socket that died under the desktop is noticed within a minute, and one address is one endpoint on the runtime. Beside the check, @jiangkaiqi2005 built the quit and the Windows update feed ([#442](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/442), [#443](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/443)), @cutey-none brought DeepSeek Harness to the Python runtime ([#433](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/433)), and @Mola-maker's two Android fixes are in ([#429](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/429), [#431](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/431)). Nothing moves for a person upgrading: the Android package installs over 1.0.4 and keeps everything, the desktop keeps its settings, and a 1.0.4 client works against the relay (0.26.0) unchanged.\n\n## Highlights\n\n- **The daily feed is written quietly, and a routine speaks first.** On Android, the iPhone and the desktop the conversation the feed is written in no longer appears in the drawer, the chat list or search, and *Write today's feed.* no longer stands anywhere as a message in your voice; on Android, posts written while the app was in the background are announced by one notification that opens the Feed. The prompt a routine sends is shown as one quiet line, *Routine · 〈label〉 · 08:00*, and the agent is told the turn is the routine's, so it opens with the result rather than thanking you for asking ([#437](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/437)).\n- **The Android approval card fits the screen, and the ChatGPT sign-in has a way through a proxy.** A long command made the card taller than the screen, so Allow, Deny and the composer sat below the bottom edge and the chat looked frozen; the card now takes at most two thirds of the screen, a command longer than six lines is folded behind *Show all*, and the buttons stay in view ([#436](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/436)). The ChatGPT sign-in sends the browser back to `localhost:1455`, which a proxy or VPN app on the phone can swallow; after ten seconds without the browser's call (at once when the phone's proxy would take the address) a note under *Sign in* explains it and offers a box to paste the address of the error page, and the code reaches the waiting sign-in without going through the proxy. The same box serves the Anthropic, xAI and OpenRouter sign-ins ([#441](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/441), both in [#449](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/449)). The sign-in's tokens stay out of the log file, the identifier field's example is an e-mail address, and two of the relay's refusals read as sentences in 17 languages.\n- **The iPhone, in detail.** The conversation scrolls under the header and fades into its scrim, as it does under the composer, and on an iPad the agent's replies line up with the composer ([#432](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/432)). Siri understands *Ask nanoMuse*, *New nanoMuse chat* and the other shortcuts in all nine languages instead of English and Chinese alone; the page titles, the agent's name and the first-run pages follow Dynamic Type; *Create routine* on an idea opens the editor; *Background & notifications* says what the phone does; a hub failure (a computer offline, busy or on an older nanoMuse) is a sentence in your language; VoiceOver names the Library's and the usage pickers and the ••• menus ([#451](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/451), [#455](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/455)). A face set to an emoji on the desktop or in the web console shows on the iPhone, after a drawn face and before the dragon, and the phone never pushes the dragon over an emoji chosen elsewhere ([#435](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/435), [#453](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/453)).\n- **The desktop does what its buttons say.** *Default face*, the clip preview's *Cancel*, Media's *Check which models answer*, the ChatGPT *Open the sign-in page*, *Sign out* and *Cancel*, and *Download* and *Reset* under Memory called the host without a body, which the window sent as a GET to routes that take POST only, so each click ended in a quiet 404; they post now, and a test checks every body-less call against the host's routes ([#438](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/438)). Quit (the menu, Ctrl+Q, the tray, or the last window without a tray) first asks what is still on: a reply being written, the hands on the screen, a task another device asked for, an approval waiting on you; *Keep running* is the default, and a confirmed quit waits for the work to end ([#442](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/442), by @jiangkaiqi2005). A hub socket that died under the app is dropped when nothing arrived between two pings, about 50 seconds, instead of after the many minutes the operating system takes; an endpoint or connector address with a password in it is refused, a redirect is followed with the key only to the endpoint's own origin; `desktop.json` is written at mode 0600; the host's refusals of a form are said in your language ([#452](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/452), [#455](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/455)).\n- **The Windows release carries the files an in-app update needs.** Beside the installer, the release has `latest.yml`, which names the installer and its SHA-512, and the installer's `.exe.blockmap`, covered by `SHA256SUMS-desktop.txt`; before anything is attached, CI hands the set to electron-updater itself, which must find the version, download the installer from a test feed and verify it ([#443](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/443), by @jiangkaiqi2005, for [#341](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/341)). The download mirror serves the feed at `nanomuse.cn/dl/win/`, pointing it at the newest release whose three files are all present and match, and leaving it on the previous release while a Windows build is still running ([#454](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/454)). The Intel Mac installer builds again, since the workflow installs pnpm from npm ([#444](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/444)).\n- **DeepSeek Harness on the runtime, and one address per endpoint.** A computer running `nanomuse serve` lists the chats of `dsh web` and DeepSeek's desktop app under `~/.dsh` beside Cursor, Codex and Claude Code, shows a transcript and sends into one with `dsh --profile headless --json`; the Muse's `coding_agents` tool takes `dsh`, and `zstandard` is a new dependency ([#433](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/433), by @cutey-none). Adding a custom endpoint at an address the list already has is refused with 409 naming the endpoint that has it, the list is changed one request at a time so a rename is no longer written over by a slower refresh, `PUT /api/connections/gui` and `/hands` check their bodies, a DingTalk stream that fails to start says so, a failed update check is tried again after an hour, the web push files are owner-only from the first byte, fetched pages are parsed off the event loop, and two more relay refusals read as sentences ([#450](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/450), [#455](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/455)).\n- **The relay's console finds anything, and a disabled account cannot be probed.** On *People* the search reaches the number or e-mail, the account id, both addresses, device names, the client and its version, the region, the inviter and the invite code, several words at once, with *Joined*, *Came* and *Version* filters beside it; `/` starts a search on any page; the account drawer's statement and timeline filter by kind and text on the relay's side; *Activity* reads on past its first page ([#440](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/440)). A code asked for a disabled account is answered with the same `204` as for anyone, and `/v1/auth/login` says `403 account_disabled` only to the right password; a wrong one is answered like any wrong password ([#447](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/447), [#455](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/455)).\n- **The web console's small text reads, and its fields have names.** The faint red, amber and grey of *overdue*, *blocked*, *failed* and the device section labels meet the contrast small text needs in both themes; the reminder, routine, trigger, goal, memory, coding, password and side-chat fields are announced by a screen reader with what they are for; a middle-click in a hands step is no longer called a right-click; the permission log shows an approval's scope in words; the hashed script and style files are cached for a year ([#448](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/448)). Outside mainland China the sign-in field's example is an e-mail address alone, and a lapsed bot sign-in says so in your language ([#455](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/455)).\n- **Android, the smaller fixes.** Styled shell output stays whole, since terminal colour and title codes are removed before carriage returns are folded ([#429](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/429), by @Mola-maker); the font-size labels under Appearance speak the app's language ([#431](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/431), by @Mola-maker); the goal-shaping prompt and the missing-image-model prompt no longer hold the agent up against another app's assistant.\n- **The showcase and the project.** A refusal of any shape from nanoMuse Cloud or the image provider reaches the browser as the refusal it was rather than a 500, and the mirror never lists half a package ([#446](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/446)); the docs describe nanoMuse in its own words, screen by screen, without another product as the model ([#445](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/445)); the READMEs' News notes the thousandth star ([#439](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/439)).\n- **TestFlight.** Build 22 (1.0.3) and build 26 (1.0.4) passed Apple's beta review on 2026-10-13, so the public link installs build 26 today; 1.0.5 goes up as build 28 and is submitted to the same review. A build reaches the link once its review has passed, the internal testers before that.\n\n## Upgrade Notes\n\n- **Android installs over 1.0.4 and keeps your data.** `nanoMuse-1.0.5-arm64.apk` (Android 8.0+, arm64; versionCode 48) is signed with the same key as every version before it. Verify with `sha256sum -c nanoMuse-1.0.5-arm64.apk.sha256`. The chat the daily feed was written in disappears from your chat list; its posts stay in the Feed.\n- **iPhone and iPad come through TestFlight.** The public link installs build 26 (1.0.4), which passed Apple's beta review with build 22 on 2026-10-13; build 28 (1.0.5) is submitted when it is uploaded, and reaches the link once its review has passed, the internal testers before that.\n- **The desktop installers are built by CI from the tag `v1.0.5`.** The Mac packages are not notarized: the first time, open the app from *System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway* (or right-click → *Open*). The Windows package is not signed: click *More info* and *Run anyway* once. On Linux prefer the `.deb`; the AppImage needs FUSE (`--appimage-extract-and-run` without). They arrive a little after the APK, and `SHA256SUMS-desktop.txt` lists every checksum. This is the first release whose Windows assets include `latest.yml` and the `.exe.blockmap`, the files electron-updater reads; the desktop's update metadata is built for `https://nanomuse.cn/dl/win/`, which the mirror points at this release once the three files are there, so a 1.0.5 desktop on Windows can take the next version from inside the app. Your settings stay where they were; the proxy file `desktop.json` is set to mode 0600 on its next write.\n- **The relay is 0.26.0; a 1.0.4 client works against it unchanged.** For operators: the console searches and filters further and reads *Activity* past its first page (`?before=` on `/v1/admin/events`, `?kind=&q=` on an account's `/ledger` and `/events`); `POST /v1/auth/code` answers `204` for a disabled account too, and `/v1/auth/login` answers `403 account_disabled` only to the right password; a `tokens` or an `n` that is not a number is a `400`; the hub's log lines carry the first twelve characters of a device id and no device name. [docs/self-hosting.md](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/blob/main/docs/self-hosting.md) and [cloud/README.md](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/blob/main/cloud/README.md) have the details.\n- **The runtime has a new dependency and refuses one thing it used to accept.** `zstandard` reads DeepSeek Harness's chat store; `pip install -e .` or the Docker image brings it. nanoMuse 1.0.4 · Compass\n\n🐉 **nanoMuse `1.0.4` “Compass”**: a health check of the whole project, a day after Helm; what nine passes over the relay, the runtime, the five clients, the showcase, the docs and the CI found is fixed here, and DeepSeek Harness joins the coding agents.\n\n1.0.3 went out on 2026-10-12. The same day we read every part of nanoMuse against every other part and against what the apps do on a phone, an iPad and a computer: the relay, the Python runtime, the web console, the desktop, the Android and iPhone apps, the hosted showcase, the documentation in both languages and the workflows that build all of it. The findings fill this version. Some you will see at once: an iPad's chat is one centred column under a frosted pill bar instead of three different widths; a rename or a new face made on one device reaches the others without a restart; a step another device's Muse asks about is answered on the iPhone where the task was typed; a screen reader hears the web console's replies. Others you will not see and should not have to: an MCP server's secrets live in the vault rather than a plain file, the Android proxy password is encrypted, a signed-out device loses its line to the hub at once, the invite bonus is paid when the friend first uses nanoMuse Cloud rather than at sign-up, every operator action on the relay is on record, and every GitHub Action is pinned to a commit. Beside the check, @cutey-none added DeepSeek Harness as a fourth coding agent on the desktop ([#354](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/354)), @brainsparker proposed You.com as a web search that needs no key ([#360](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/360)), @Ichiro786 blended the Android chat's navigation surround ([#397](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/397)), and @Mola-maker's reports and fixes on the Android app's speech input and tests are in ([#356](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/356), [#394](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/394), [#405](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/405)). Nothing moves for a person upgrading: the Android package installs over 1.0.3 and keeps everything, the desktop keeps its settings, and a 1.0.3 client works against the relay (0.25.0) unchanged.\n\n## Highlights\n\n- **The iPad's chat is one column, and the pill bar is glass again.** On an iPad the messages, the composer and the pill bar share one centred column of 760 pt, the web console's width; the composer and the pill bar are exactly as wide as each other, and the agent's replies grow from a 340 pt pill to 600 pt. The conversation now scrolls under the composer and the pill bar on every iPhone and iPad, so the bar blurs the rows behind it as it blurs the Feed and the Library, and a fade of the canvas colour rises above the composer while older messages are being read; in 1.0.3 the bar sat on a plain canvas and read as a solid pill, and the last message was cut off at the composer's top edge. A side chat's header dissolves like the main chat's, Ideas, Goals and the Library stand on the chat's canvas, and Reduce Motion is honoured throughout: the pill bar's indicator moves without the spring, the face keeps still, the slides, the drawer and the bottom bar crossfade ([#406](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/406), [#411](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/411), [#423](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/423)).\n- **Your devices agree with each other.** Signing in on an iPhone brings the account's chats, name and face down at once, instead of after a trip to the background; a rename or a connection made on a phone without a face of its own no longer puts the dragon over the account's face on every other device; the name and the face another device changed arrive when the app comes back to the front; a chat older than a week can be renamed again and the title follows; a fresh device joins the account's main chat on its first pull instead of starting a second one; and the model's hidden notes stay out of the synced chat. On Android a chat model picked under *Settings › Models* answers the main chat's first message too, a group picked in a chat's picker is the default for new chats with the group's thinking level, and signing in to another account starts from that account's own name and face ([#408](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/408), [#409](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/409), [#410](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/410), [#421](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/421)).\n- **A step another device's Muse asks about is answered on the iPhone.** A task sent with `@〈device〉` runs on that device's Muse; when a step there needs a yes, the question used to be declined from the phone with a line telling you to approve it over there. The phone now shows the card where the task was typed, with the Android phone's four answers: *Allow once*, *Allow for this chat*, *Always allow this on 〈device〉* (listed with *Revoke* under *Approvals* on the agent's page) and *Deny*; a payment gets only once and deny, no answer within the time the other side allows counts as a no, and a question answered first at the other device closes the card ([#424](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/424)).\n- **DeepSeek Harness is a fourth coding agent.** The *Coding agents* page on the desktop, and from the phone over the hub, knew Cursor, Codex and Claude Code; the chats of `dsh web` and DeepSeek's desktop app under `~/.dsh` are now listed beside them, a transcript is shown, and a message is sent into one with `dsh --profile headless --json`, through a `dsh` on `PATH` or else the harness the app ships. The store is zstd written one frame at a time, and every frame is read. Written by @cutey-none ([#354](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/354)); the Python runtime does not list dsh yet.\n- **A web search that needs no key.** `provider = \"you\"` under `[connectors.search]`, or the You.com chip under *Connections → Web search*, searches You.com without an account, 100 times a day per address; past that the result says so and DuckDuckGo answers once. A key of your own moves the searches to the keyed API with higher limits, and the Sentinel shows whichever host is in use. DuckDuckGo stays the default. Proposed by @brainsparker ([#360](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/360)).\n- **Secrets where they belong.** An MCP server's `env` values typed in the app went into `app-settings.json` as plain text; each now goes into the encrypted vault as `MCP_<SERVER>_<KEY>` and the file keeps a reference, and the web console's MCP form has an *Environment* field that says so. An endpoint address with a password in it is refused, a key is no longer sent to a host that was not named when an endpoint redirects, and `nanomuse config show` masks every kind of credential. The Android proxy password moves to an encrypted file, the iPhone's to the keychain, a password saved by 1.0.3 is moved over on the first read. Creating a reminder, a trigger or a goal counts as a change, so `strict` mode asks first; the browser refuses the carrier-grade NAT range with the other private ranges; a calendar feed that fails no longer shows its private link ([#387](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/387), [#416](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/416), [#421](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/421), [#423](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/423)).\n- **The relay keeps better books.** The invite bonus is paid when the invited friend first uses nanoMuse Cloud, not at sign-up, so padding a pool with throwaway accounts no longer pays; the admin page shows who invited whom, names the inviters worth a look and has one action for them; every operator action on an account is on record; a disabled account is told so before a code is sent; deleting an account forgets it at once; a device that is signed out loses its hub socket the same moment, so a lost phone cannot reach the account's other devices meanwhile; the web console open in two tabs no longer fights itself on the hub; `TRUSTED_PROXIES` narrows the per-address limits too; backups take a consistent copy and can be read by the deploying user ([#384](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/384), [#391](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/391), [#401](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/401), [#413](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/413)).\n- **The web console reads aloud and takes the keyboard.** A screen reader hears that the agent is writing and reads the reply once it is complete; the menus open on their first entry, walk with the arrow keys and close on Escape; the browser viewer scrolls with the keys; the tool calling chips are translated and the chosen one is marked; the feed and a skill say when they could not load, with *Try again*; adding an MCP server with its tools marked *high* no longer fails, since the chip is *sensitive*, the level the runtime knows ([#382](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/382), [#414](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/pull/414)).\n- **Android, fixed where it broke.** A Claude sign-in no longer closes the app: the provider refuses the send with one sentence, and a build without the identifier does not offer the sign-in ([#373](https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse/issues/373), reported by @moh8919-dev). Remembering a payment approval no longer closes the app either, since the manifest now declares the permission the screen lock needs.
